shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on an airline flight, departing an airport in high terrain in the evening. Hot, with a high density altitude and moderate turbulence forecast.

The crew. The first officer, with about 4,700 hours, was the pilot flying; the captain, with about 4,430, the pilot monitoring. Neither pilot was familiar with the airport.

What happened. Before departure the crew received a route change by datalink, which they loaded, executed and accepted together. This removed the departure procedure from the flight plan, though the runway stayed on the display; the operating manual describes this effect. Neither pilot noticed; they had checked the departure during the initial set-up and did not check it again. A complex engine-failure procedure, briefed at length, added fixes, distance rings and radials to the navigation display. Slow engine starts in the heat added distraction. At take-off an unforecast crosswind gusted to 19 knots, and another aircraft was cleared to land behind them. After take-off they were cleared to climb unrestricted to flight level 190. During flap retraction the first officer selected vertical navigation and direct climb and engaged the autopilot. The aircraft turned right towards the next fix in the computer, earlier than the departure's right turn. The first officer thought this seemed odd but put it down to the unrestricted climb. The controller then gave a low altitude alert and asked which departure they were assigned. The captain named it; the controller gave heading 360, and the first officer selected it.
safe_outcome: The aircraft turned onto the assigned heading, and the flight continued to its cruising altitude. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: both reporters' debriefs, 'due to inexperience', 'we failed to trap the error', 'I should have reloaded the SID', 'I should have recognized', 'incorrectly attributed', 'I am so disappointed and embarrassed', the agreed preventive measures and 'better CRM habits', and the praise of the first officer's briefing. Kept as facts at the time or confirmed afterwards: the route change dropping the departure (confirmed afterwards), that the runway stayed displayed, that the operating manual describes this effect, that the departure was checked at initial set-up but not after the route change (stated by both reporters), the engine-failure procedure's added display items, the slow starts, the unforecast gusting crosswind, the landing traffic, the early right turn (narrative 2: 'too early, but in the same direction as the SID') and the first officer's thought at the time that it seemed odd. Moved to the safe ending (rule 5): the turn onto the assigned heading and the continued flight. Left out of the safe ending: the controller's request that the crew contact the approach facility, which they did after the flight; it would appear in one version only. Removed under rule 6: the departure and fix names, the runway and the airport. Cut for length: arriving early, taxiway closures, the exact wind, turbulence forecast up to 13,000 ft, the take-off thrust setting and the control handover after line-up. Judgement calls: time of day given only as the local band 1801-2400, so 'in the evening'; one narrative ties the early turn to the flight director and the other to engaging the autopilot, so the text says only that the aircraft turned. Bracket 'crossing' because the deviation was an early lateral turn off the departure track.
